Traits: Hooked raptorial bill with a fleshy cere; powerful feet with long curved talons and an enlarged killing hallux; forward-set eyes with acute vision and a bony brow ridge; broad soaring wings; reversed size dimorphism (females larger).

Seed plants whose ovules and seeds sit exposed on the surface of a scale or leaf ('naked seeds'), not enclosed in a fruit; wind pollination with a pollination droplet; mostly woody; simple tracheid-only xylem in conifers.
Skeleton-less solitary hexacorals (sea anemones) that attach and burrow with a muscular pedal disc; a crown of tentacles; many have defensive acontia or elongated catch-tentacles.

Coelacanths: a three-lobed (trilobed) tail with a small central lobe, a hinged intracranial joint letting the front of the skull swing up, an oil-filled notochord in place of vertebral centra, and paired lobed fins; 'living fossils'.

Ray-finned fishes: fins webbed between bony rays (lepidotrichia) with little muscle extending into them, a single dorsal fin ancestrally, and a swim bladder for buoyancy; by far the most species-rich vertebrate group.

The great water-associated radiation (shorebirds, gulls, plovers, flamingos, grebes, loons, penguins, tubenoses, herons, pelicans); convergent aquatic adaptations - supraorbital salt glands, dense waterproof plumage, webbed or lobed feet - rather than one shared skeletal trait.
The 'Africa-origin' landbird clade (accipitrids, owls, mousebirds, trogons, hornbills, rollers, woodpeckers); ancestrally predatory; cavity nesting and semi-zygodactyl feet are widespread.

A placental clade of African origin - elephants, hyraxes, sea cows, aardvark, tenrecs, elephant shrews, golden moles; unusually many thoracolumbar vertebrae, late-erupting permanent teeth, and testes that stay in the abdomen (testicondy).

The mushroom lineage: fungi that build large fleshy or woody fruiting bodies with the spore layer on gills, pores or teeth; the principal decomposers of wood, including the white-rot fungi that are the main organisms able to break down lignin; also many ectomycorrhizal partners.

Bulky folivorous atelids with an enlarged hyoid bone forming a resonating throat chamber that produces roaring calls audible for kilometres; a prehensile tail; a sluggish, energy-conserving lifestyle; some have routine trichromatic colour vision.

Traits: The non-flagellated fungi (zygomycetes plus Dikarya): the flagellum and centriole are lost, so dispersal is entirely by non-motile spores carried on air or water or by animals.
Echinoderms plus hemichordates; a three-part coelom (proto-, meso-, metacoel), a dipleurula-type ciliated larva, and (ancestrally) a water vascular system derived from the mesocoel.

Tetrapods that reproduce on land via an amniotic egg (amnion, chorion, allantois) or its live-bearing derivative; a waterproof keratinised (cornified) skin; costal (rib) breathing; no aquatic larval stage.

Amoebae and slime moulds with blunt, tubular (lobose) pseudopodia and 'fountain' cytoplasmic streaming; tubular mitochondrial cristae; at most a single posterior flagellum; includes Amoeba and Dictyostelium.

Amoebozoa + Obazoa (amoebae, slime moulds, breviates, apusomonads, fungi and animals); cells ancestrally with a single posterior flagellum and/or amoeboid movement ('unikont' organisation); no strict morphological synapomorphy.

Flowering plants: ovules enclosed in a carpel that ripens into a fruit, flowers, double fertilisation producing a nutritive triploid endosperm, vessels in the xylem, sieve-tube/companion-cell phloem, and a very reduced gametophyte (an 8-nucleate embryo sac).
Segmented worms with a body of repeated ring-like segments separated by septa, a spacious coelom acting as a hydrostatic skeleton, chitinous bristles (chaetae), and a closed circulatory system.
Broad flattened bill lined with filtering lamellae; palmate (webbed) feet; dense waterproof plumage with thick down and an enlarged uropygial gland; males retain an intromittent phallus.

Bryophytes with a thin thallus whose cells often each contain a single large chloroplast with a pyrenoid (a carbon-concentrating feature unique among land plants), and a needle-like sporophyte that grows continuously from a basal meristem and splits lengthwise.
Cnidarians with only the polyp stage (no medusa); the gut is partitioned by mesenteries and opens through a folded pharynx (actinopharynx); linear mitochondrial DNA; sea anemones and corals.

Frogs and toads: no tail as adults, a short spine with a long rod-like urostyle, hugely elongated hindlimbs and fused ankle bones for jumping, a fused radioulna and tibiofibula, and a large eardrum; vocal males.

Night (owl) monkeys - the only nocturnal anthropoids: huge brown eyes with no fovea and a monochromatic retina, a non-prehensile tail, monogamous pairs with heavy paternal carrying of infants, and scent communication.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Aphelids: tiny intracellular parasites (parasitoids) of algae; a walled resting spore, an amoeboid or flagellate infective stage that enters the host and phagocytoses its contents from within, then fills the host cell with a plasmodium.
Gliding biflagellate bacterivores with a dorsal organic shell (theca) and a cytoplasmic sleeve wrapped around the base of the anterior flagellum.
Mostly terrestrial chelicerates with four pairs of walking legs, book lungs and/or tracheae, malpighian tubules, and often silk or venom glands; pedipalps modified for sensing or prey capture.

Prokaryotes with ether-linked, branched isoprenoid membrane lipids and cell walls lacking peptidoglycan; DNA replication, transcription and translation machinery resembling that of eukaryotes; histone-like proteins; many extremophiles.

Eukaryotes whose plastid came directly from primary endosymbiosis of a cyanobacterium (two envelope membranes, no periplastid compartment); red algae, green algae + land plants, and glaucophytes; starch/floridean-starch storage.
Turtles plus archosaurs (crocodiles and birds); shared microRNA and chromosomal characters; ancestrally with a diapsid skull (secondarily closed in turtles).
'Ruling reptiles': an antorbital fenestra in the skull, teeth set in sockets (thecodont), a four-chambered heart, and often an upright limb posture; crocodile-line and bird-line reptiles.
The 'bear-like' caniforms - bears, pinnipeds, and the weasel/raccoon/skunk/red-panda group; united by features of the ossified auditory bulla and skull base, and an ancestrally plantigrade foot.
Ecdysozoans with a segmented body and jointed limbs, a hardened chitinous exoskeleton, an open haemocoel with a dorsal heart, a ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia, and compound eyes.

Even-toed ungulates: weight borne equally on the third and fourth toes, a distinctive 'double-pulley' astragalus (ankle bone) allowing a very flexible foot; includes pigs, camels, ruminants, hippos and - nested within - the cetaceans.

Sac fungi: sexual spores (classically eight) formed by meiosis inside a cylindrical sac, the ascus, and usually shot out; abundant asexual spores (conidia); the fungal partner of most lichens; yeasts, moulds (Penicillium, Aspergillus), morels, truffles.

The other big eudicot clade (~1/3 of angiosperms): usually with petals fused into a tube, a fixed low number of stamens attached to the corolla, ovules with a single integument and a thin nucellus, and iridoid or alkaloid chemistry; heathers, coffee, nightshades, mints, sunflowers.
Sea stars: broad arms merging into the disc, open ambulacral grooves with suckered tube feet, the ability to evert the stomach to feed externally, and strong arm regeneration.
Star-shaped echinoderms with arms radiating from a central disc: sea stars and brittle stars; ambulacral grooves running out along the underside of each arm.
The largest New World monkeys - howlers, spider, woolly and muriqui monkeys - all with a strongly prehensile tail bearing a naked, friction-ridged gripping pad on its underside, used as a fifth limb.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Long-limbed acrobatic atelids with a hook-like hand whose thumb is reduced or absent (aiding brachiation), a highly prehensile tail, a fruit-heavy diet, and fission-fusion social groups.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Placentals of Gondwanan (South American + African) origin: the xenarthrans plus Afrotheria; the grouping is mainly molecular and biogeographic.
The 'southern' core landbirds (seriemas, falcons, parrots, passerines); ancestrally raptorial; the parrot + passerine subclade shows extreme brain enlargement and vocal learning.
Toothless keratinous beak; no teeth; short tail ending in a plough-shaped pygostyle; fused synsacrum; large keeled sternum and furcula; flow-through air-sac lungs; feathers with an aftershaft.

Prokaryotes with peptidoglycan (murein) cell walls and ester-linked fatty-acid membranes; bacterial-type RNA polymerase and 70S ribosomes; formyl-methionine translation start; usually one circular chromosome; no nucleus.

Club fungi: sexual spores (usually four) budded externally on a club-shaped cell, the basidium, after meiosis; a long-lived dikaryotic mycelium often with clamp connections; complex fruiting bodies in many; mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs, rusts and smuts.

Skates and rays: dorsoventrally flattened, pectoral fins hugely enlarged and fused to the head as a disc, gill slits on the underside, eyes and spiracles on top, and (in many) a whip-like tail with a venomous barb.
Ancestrally biflagellate eukaryotes; encompasses most photosynthetic and free-living protist lineages; molecularly circumscribed, no morphological synapomorphy.

Animals with bilateral symmetry (at least in the larva), three germ layers including a true mesoderm, anterior concentration of nerves and sense organs (cephalisation), and a through-gut in most; Hox genes in a colinear cluster.

Molluscs with a two-part hinged shell closed by adductor muscles, no head or radula, large sheet-like gills used for filter feeding, and a hatchet-shaped burrowing foot; clams, mussels, oysters, scallops.
The 'northern' placentals: Laurasiatheria (carnivores, ungulates, bats, etc.) plus Euarchontoglires (primates, rodents, rabbits); mainly a molecular clade, of Laurasian origin.
Small anaerobic amoeboflagellates with two flagella and filose pseudopodia; mitochondrion-related organelles adapted to low oxygen.

Non-vascular land plants - mosses, liverworts, hornworts: a dominant photosynthetic gametophyte with a small, unbranched, nutritionally dependent sporophyte bearing a single sporangium; no true xylem/phloem, roots or leaves; swimming sperm needing a film of water.

Bryophytes with spirally arranged one-cell-thick leaves on a radial stem, rhizoids for anchorage, an elaborate spore capsule with a toothed peristome and operculum for gradual spore release, and conducting cells (hydroids/leptoids).
Molecular clade uniting Archaeplastida with Cryptista (and Microheliella); relevant to the spread of red-algal-derived plastids; no morphological synapomorphy.
The clade uniting Ceratophyllales with the monocots and eudicots - i.e. most flowering-plant species; a molecular grouping within the core angiosperms.
Small clade named as an acronym for Collodictyonidae, Rigifilida and Mantamonas; ventrally-grooved or gliding flagellates with filose pseudopodia.
Sponges whose spicules are calcium carbonate (calcite); the only sponges to show all three aquiferous grades (asconoid, syconoid, leuconoid); choanocytes with the nucleus at the flagellar base.
Titi monkeys: small monogamous pitheciids that sleep and sit with tails entwined, defend territories with dawn duets, show intense male infant care, and eat mostly fruit supplemented with leaves.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Marmosets and tamarins: the smallest anthropoids, with claw-like nails on all digits except the big toe, usually twin births, cooperative care by the group, and (in marmosets) chisel teeth for gouging tree bark to feed on gum.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Camels, llamas and relatives: two toes on broad padded feet (not true hooves), a pacing gait, oval nucleated red blood cells, a three-chambered ruminating stomach, splayed upper lip, and fat stored in humps or the body.
The campanulid (euasterid II) clade: bellflowers, sunflowers and the whole daisy family, hollies, ivies, carrots; often with inferior ovaries and early-fusing ('early sympetaly') corollas.

Dogs, wolves and foxes: long-legged, digitigrade endurance hunters with blunt non-retractile claws and a long muzzle carrying many teeth (shearing carnassials but also crushing molars for omnivory); cooperative pack living and pair bonding in many.

Dog-line carnivorans: a longer snout, more numerous and less specialised teeth, usually non-retractile claws, a single-chambered auditory bulla, and a baculum; dogs, bears, weasels, raccoons, red panda, and the seals.

Placental predators (and their omnivore/herbivore descendants) with a pair of shearing carnassial teeth (last upper premolar against first lower molar), usually large canines, a reduced or fused clavicle, and a well-developed sense of smell.

Old World monkeys and apes: narrow downward-facing nostrils close together, two premolars per quadrant, a bony ear tube (tubular ectotympanic), routine trichromatic colour vision, and no prehensile tail.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Salamanders and newts: a lizard-like body with a long tail kept as adults, four limbs of roughly equal size held out to the sides, the ability to regenerate limbs and tail, and internal fertilisation via a spermatophore in most.

New World monkeys comprising capuchins and squirrel monkeys (plus the callitrichids in broad usage): agile, large-brained, highly manipulative omnivores; capuchins have a weakly prehensile tail, squirrel monkeys a non-prehensile one.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Stocky, exceptionally large-brained New World monkeys with a semi-prehensile tail carried coiled, strong hands, extractive foraging, documented tool use (stone hammers, anvils) and fur-rubbing behaviour.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Small fish-like filter-feeders (amphioxus) that keep all chordate features as adults: a notochord running the whole body length (into the head), no true head, brain or paired eyes, and a large pharyngeal basket in an atrium.

Active marine molluscs with the foot modified into arms/tentacles around the mouth, a chambered buoyancy shell (external, internal or lost), jet propulsion from the funnel, a beak, closed circulation, and large image-forming eyes.
The tapir + rhinoceros branch of odd-toed ungulates; ancestrally with four toes on the forefoot and three on the hind, and a tendency toward large body size and browsing.

Hornworts of the pond (Ceratophyllum): rootless submerged aquatic plants with whorls of brittle forked leaves, water pollination, and one of the oldest angiosperm fossil records; sister to the eudicots in many analyses.

Old World monkeys: bilophodont molars (paired transverse ridges), sitting pads of hardened skin (ischial callosities), often cheek pouches for storing food, a tail that is never prehensile, and narrow chests with limbs built for quadrupedal walking.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: The cheek-pouched Old World monkeys - macaques, baboons, mangabeys, guenons, vervets: large distensible cheek pouches, a simple stomach, a more omnivorous diet, and often terrestrial, large-group living with pronounced male-biased size.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Fully aquatic artiodactyls: a hairless streamlined body, forelimbs as flippers and no external hindlimbs, a horizontal tail fluke, a blowhole on top of the skull with telescoped facial bones, blubber, and nursing underwater.
Ruminants together with the hippo + whale clade (Whippomorpha); a molecular grouping within even-toed ungulates.

The freshwater green algae most closely related to land plants (e.g. Zygnematophyceae, Charophyceae, Coleochaetophyceae); phragmoplast cell division, plasmodesmata and rosette cellulose synthases in some - features inherited by land plants. A paraphyletic grade.
Arthropods whose body is a prosoma (bearing chelicerae, pedipalps and four leg pairs) plus an opisthosoma; no antennae; no mandibles; often book lungs or book gills; extra-oral digestion.
Fast predatory myriapods, dorsoventrally flattened, with one leg pair per trunk segment and a pair of venomous fang-like forcipules (modified first legs); long antennae.

The only truly flying mammals: forelimbs modified into wings with a skin membrane (patagium) stretched between very long finger bones, a keeled sternum, hind feet turned to hang upside down, and laryngeal echolocation in most.

A small early-diverging angiosperm lineage (Chloranthaceae) of aromatic herbs and shrubs with swollen leaf nodes, toothed opposite leaves, and tiny reduced flowers; abundant in the Early Cretaceous pollen record.
One of the two main green-algal clades, mostly marine; motile cells typically with two equal apical flagella on a cross-shaped (cruciate) root system; includes Chlamydomonas and sea lettuce (Ulva).
Solitary or colonial bacterivores, each cell driving water with one flagellum through a collar of actin-supported microvilli that strains out bacteria; the closest living relatives of animals.

Cartilaginous fishes with a prismatic calcified cartilage skeleton, no true bone, tooth-like placoid scales (dermal denticles), teeth in replacement rows, claspers for internal fertilisation, and no swim bladder.
Animals with, at some life stage, a dorsal notochord, a hollow dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, an endostyle/thyroid, and a post-anal tail with segmented (myomeric) muscle blocks.

A (probably non-monophyletic) grouping of algae and their relatives with red-algal-derived plastids inside four membranes or a periplastid compartment - diatoms, brown algae, dinoflagellates, cryptomonads, haptophytes - together with many secondarily non-photosynthetic lineages (ciliates, oomycetes, foraminifera).

Chytrids: the main fungi that keep a single posterior whiplash flagellum, on motile zoospores that swim to new substrates; mostly aquatic or soil saprotrophs and parasites; includes Batrachochytrium, the cause of global amphibian declines.
Armoured xenarthrans (armadillos, extinct glyptodonts) with a shell of bony dermal plates (osteoderms) covered in horn, often with movable bands; strong digging forelimbs and simple peg teeth.
Radial animals with one gut opening, two body layers, and stinging cnidocytes that fire a coiled nematocyst thread; a nerve net; a life cycle alternating polyp and medusa.

Cephalopods with the shell reduced, internalised (gladius, cuttlebone, phragmocone) or lost; eight or ten sucker-bearing arms; chromatophore skin for instant colour and pattern change; large complex brains and camera eyes; an ink sac; short lives ending in a single reproductive event.

Leaf-eating Old World monkeys - colobus, langurs, proboscis and snub-nosed monkeys: a large multi-chambered ('ruminant-like') foregut-fermenting stomach, high-crested shearing molars, reduced or absent thumb in colobus, and long tails and limbs for leaping.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: A landbird assemblage of doves, sandgrouse, mesites, turacos, cuckoos and bustards; ancestrally granivorous/frugivorous ground and canopy feeders; clade support is chiefly molecular.

Syndactyl feet, with the front toes fused along part of their length; large head on a short neck with a long, often dagger-like bill; nest in burrows or cavities; naked altricial chicks; frequently iridescent plumage.

Terrestrial burrowing annelids (oligochaetes) with few chaetae, no parapodia or head appendages, a glandular clitellum that secretes an egg cocoon, hermaphroditism, and a gut adapted to processing soil.

Stalked or free 'sea lilies' and feather stars: mouth and anus both face upward on a cup (calyx) with feeding arms bearing a ciliated food groove; the only living echinoderms with the mouth on the upper surface.
Nucleariid filose amoebae plus Fonticula (a cellular slime mould); naked or scale-covered cells with fine radiating filopodia; sister to Fungi.

Semi-aquatic archosaurs with heavy bony-plated (osteoderm) armour, a secondary bony palate, a sprawling-to-'high walk' gait, a muscular valved four-chambered heart, parental care, and a slap-shut death roll.
Mostly aquatic mandibulates with two pairs of antennae, biramous (two-branched) limbs, gills, a nauplius larva, and calcified cuticle in many; crabs, shrimp, copepods, barnacles, woodlice.

Hidden-necked turtles: the neck retracts in a vertical S-bend to pull the head straight back into the shell; the pelvis is not fused to the shell; sea turtles, tortoises, snapping turtles, softshells - most living turtle diversity.

Biradial gelatinous predators that swim using eight rows of fused giant cilia (comb rows) - the largest animals to move by cilia; sticky colloblast cells capture prey; an aboral statocyst; a muscular mesoglea.

'Box jellies': a cuboidal medusa with camera-type lensed eyes on four rhopalia, muscular pedalia carrying the tentacles, a true velarium, and potent venom; the polyp metamorphoses entirely into a single medusa.

Palm-like gymnosperms with a stout unbranched trunk, a crown of tough pinnate leaves, coralloid roots housing nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, huge cones, motile (swimming) sperm, and dioecy; living genera radiated only in the last ~12 million years.

Living jawless vertebrates (lampreys + hagfishes): no jaws, no paired fins, a single median nostril, a cartilaginous skeleton with no bone, a notochord retained through life, and a rasping keratinous tongue apparatus.

Ten-appendage coleoids - squids and cuttlefishes - with eight arms plus two longer retractile prey-catching tentacles, an internal chitinous pen or a chambered cuttlebone, lateral fins for steady swimming, fast jet escape, and a streamlined pelagic body.
The largest sponge class; skeleton of silica spicules that are never six-rayed and/or of spongin fibres; leuconoid canal system; includes bath sponges and rock-boring sponges.

Bilaterians in which (ancestrally) the blastopore becomes the anus and the mouth forms secondarily, cleavage is radial, the mesoderm and coelom form by enterocoely, and pharyngeal gill slits are present.
Huge molecular clade (Archaeplastida + SAR + Haptista + Cryptista and kin) containing most photosynthetic eukaryotes; no morphological synapomorphy.

The 'higher fungi' (Ascomycota + Basidiomycota): a prolonged dikaryon stage with two distinct unfused haploid nuclei per cell, regularly septate hyphae with pored cross-walls, croziers or clamp connections at cell division, and large complex fruiting bodies.
Slow detritivorous myriapods, cylindrical, with two leg pairs per apparent segment (diplosegments), short antennae, and defensive glands (some producing cyanide); among the first animals on land.

Lungfishes: obligate or facultative air-breathers with paired or single lungs, crushing tooth plates fused to the palate, an autostylic jaw (no separate upper jaw bone), a largely cartilaginous braincase, and aestivation in mud.
Eukaryotes whose mitochondria have distinctive discoid (plate-like) cristae; mostly free-living flagellates; unites Euglenozoa and Percolozoa.

Protostomes with a cuticle (often chitinous) shed by moulting under hormonal control; no locomotory cilia on the body surface; growth in steps between moults; includes arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades.

Marine deuterostomes with fivefold (pentaradial) adult symmetry from a bilateral larva, a calcite endoskeleton of porous ossicles (stereom), a water vascular system operating tube feet, and mutable collagenous tissue.
Sea urchins and sand dollars: ossicles fused into a rigid test bearing movable spines on ball-and-socket joints, a five-toothed jaw apparatus (Aristotle's lantern), and pedicellariae.
Globular or cylindrical echinoderms with no arms: sea urchins and sea cucumbers; body built on five ambulacra running from mouth to the opposite pole.
Sharks, skates and rays: five to seven separate gill slits, a spiracle, a rigid upper jaw only loosely attached to the braincase (hyostyly), and ampullae of Lorenzini for electroreception.
Free-living echinoderms (all living classes except crinoids); mouth directed downward or to one side; tube feet used for locomotion; a madreporite opening the water vascular system to the exterior.
Obligately parasitic cnidarians (Myxozoa + Polypodium) reduced to a few cells, yet retaining polar capsules homologous to nematocysts.

Horses, asses and zebras: a single functional hoofed toe per foot (side toes reduced to splint bones), very long limbs with a passive stay apparatus for standing/sleeping, high-crowned grinding teeth, and long-distance running.

Horsetails (Equisetum): jointed, hollow, silica-impregnated ('scouring rush') stems with whorls of tiny fused scale leaves and whorled branches, spores borne on umbrella-shaped sporangiophores in a terminal cone, and spores with moisture-sensitive coiling straps (elaters).
Primates together with treeshrews and (in some analyses) colugos; ancestrally small arboreal mammals with grasping feet and an emphasis on vision.
The placental clade of primates, treeshrews and colugos (Euarchonta) plus rodents and rabbits (Glires); mostly a molecular grouping, ancestrally small and arboreal.
The core asterids (lamiids + campanulids): sympetalous flowers with the stamens alternating with the corolla lobes, and a strong tendency to fuse flower parts and reduce their number.

Flowering plants with pollen having three apertures (tricolpate) - a trait with a sharp ~125-million-year-old fossil first appearance; usually two seed leaves, net-veined leaves, flower parts in fours or fives, a taproot, and a vascular cambium giving true wood.

Flagellates with two flagella emerging from an apical pocket, a lattice-like paraxonemal rod alongside each axoneme, discoid cristae, and a proteinaceous pellicle of strips; includes euglenids and the kinetoplastids (trypanosomes).

Cells with a membrane-bound nucleus and endomembrane system; mitochondria from an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont; an actin/tubulin cytoskeleton; linear chromosomes packaged on histones; 80S ribosomes; mitosis and meiotic sex.

Small, mostly insectivorous laurasiatheres - shrews, moles, hedgehogs, solenodons; a long pointed mobile snout, small eyes, primitive sharp-cusped (zalambdodont/dilambdodont) molars, and a reduced or absent caecum; venomous saliva in several.
Animals with true epithelia sealed by belt junctions over a basement membrane, a gut, and ancestrally nerve and sensory cells arranged on a defined body symmetry.

The 'true fungi': a chitinous cell wall present throughout the life cycle, growth as absorptive hyphae or yeasts, and reproduction by non-motile spores (the flagellum is retained only in the basal chytrid lineages and lost above them).

Vascular plants with true megaphyll leaves (a branched vein system, from flattened and webbed branch systems), sporangia in clusters, and a distinctive small loop (pseudoendospory) in early xylem; ferns plus seed plants.
The core of the rosid radiation, split into the fabids and malvids; a rapid Cretaceous diversification producing most rosid families.

Placental mammals: a long pregnancy nourished by a chorioallantoic placenta, no epipubic bones (allowing a distensible abdomen), a corpus callosum linking the brain hemispheres, and relatively well-developed newborns.

Hoofed placental mammals - odd-toed (horses, tapirs, rhinos) and even-toed (pigs, ruminants, hippos, whales); the digit tips bear hooves, limbs are built for running with reduced side toes, and most are herbivores with complex stomachs or an enlarged caecum.

The fabid (eurosid I / nitrogen-fixing) clade: legumes, roses, figs, oaks, willows, cucurbits, spurges; contains almost all plants able to form root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria (the 'nitrogen-fixing clade').

Hooked bill with a pointed 'tomial tooth' notch for severing prey vertebrae (prey killed by bite, not talons); dark eyes and no bony brow ridge; long pointed wings; active flapping flight; a distinct moult sequence.

Cat-like carnivorans (Feliformia): a shorter face, fewer teeth with more specialised carnassials, often retractile claws, a double-chambered bony auditory bulla, and grooming with the forepaw; cats, hyenas, mongooses, civets.
Carnivora plus Pholidota (pangolins); ancestrally predatory or insectivorous mammals; share features of the ankle and skull base.
Carnivorans and pangolins together with the hoofed mammals (odd- and even-toed ungulates, including cetaceans); a molecular grouping within Scrotifera.

Sloths: slow arboreal (or, when extinct, giant ground) xenarthrans with long hooked claws for hanging upside down, extra neck vertebrae in some, a multi-chambered stomach for leaves, very low metabolism, and grooved hair that hosts algae.

Osmotrophic eukaryotes that digest food externally with secreted enzymes and absorb the products; cell walls containing chitin; glycogen as storage; a haploid-dominant life cycle; no plastids or phagotrophy in most; includes highly reduced parasites at its base.

Short, stout, slightly down-curved bill; heavy body, short rounded wings and explosive burst flight; strong feet with blunt claws for scratching; large crop and muscular gizzard; often bare facial skin, combs or wattles.
Basal neognaths ('fowl'); precocial, downy, nidifugous chicks; shared derived features of the skull and pelvis (support is largely molecular).

Molluscs that undergo torsion as larvae, twisting the visceral mass 180 deg so the mantle cavity faces forward; a single (often coiled) shell; a well-developed head with tentacles and a radula; snails, slugs, limpets.

A single living species, Ginkgo biloba: a tree with fan-shaped, forked-veined deciduous leaves, short spur shoots, swimming sperm, and fleshy foul-smelling seed coats; unchanged in form for ~200 million years - a 'living fossil'.
Freshwater algae retaining the most cyanobacterium-like plastid (a 'muroplast' or cyanelle) with a vestigial peptidoglycan wall between its membranes and carboxysome-like inclusions; phycobilisomes.

Rodents plus lagomorphs: a pair of ever-growing, self-sharpening chisel-like incisors in each jaw, no canines, and a wide toothless gap (diastema) before the cheek teeth, with the jaw able to slide forward to gnaw or back to chew.

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi: obligate root symbionts of most land plants, growing tree-like feeding structures (arbuscules) inside root cortex cells; coenocytic hyphae, giant multinucleate spores, no known sexual stage; partners in the plant colonisation of land.

Jawed vertebrates: jaws from the first pharyngeal arch, teeth with dentine and enamel, paired pectoral and pelvic fins/limbs, three semicircular canals, a myelin sheath on nerves, and an adaptive immune system.

An odd gymnosperm group of three very different genera - Ephedra (jointed desert shrubs), Gnetum (broadleaf tropical vines/trees) and Welwitschia (two ever-growing strap leaves): vessel elements in the xylem and flower-like compound cones, features convergent with angiosperms.

Gorillas: the largest living primates, ground-dwelling knuckle-walkers with extreme male size and a sagittal skull crest, a folivorous hindgut-fermenting diet, cohesive one-male ('silverback') groups, and 48 chromosomes.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Marsh and grassland birds (rails, crakes, cranes, finfoots); laterally compressed body and long toes for moving through dense vegetation; reduced tail; frequent evolution of island flightlessness; precocial dark downy chicks.

Caecilians: limbless, near-blind burrowing (or aquatic) amphibians with a ringed (annulated) body, a solid braincase, a pair of chemosensory tentacles between eye and nostril, and dermal scales in the skin folds of many.
A proposed (and much-disputed) grouping of haptophytes (coccolithophores) with cryptophytes and kin; if real, united only by molecular data - the two groups differ greatly in structure.

'Dry-nosed' primates - tarsiers, monkeys and apes: no rhinarium and a mobile continuous upper lip, no tapetum, a retinal fovea for sharp central vision, a single-chambered uterus, a haemochorial placenta, and an inability to make their own vitamin C.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Marine worms (acorn worms) and colonial pterobranchs with a body of proboscis, collar and trunk, pharyngeal gill slits, a stomochord (a buccal diverticulum once thought a notochord), and a dorsal collar nerve cord.
Anthozoans whose tentacles and mesenteries come in multiples of six; simple unarmoured nematocysts; includes reef-building stony corals (aragonite skeleton), sea anemones and zoanthids.
Deep-sea 'glass sponges' with a skeleton of six-rayed (triaxonic) silica spicules, often fused into a rigid lattice; body largely one giant multinucleate syncytium that conducts electrical impulses.
Six-legged pancrustaceans with the body in head, thorax (three leg-bearing segments) and abdomen; one pair of antennae; tracheal breathing; malpighian tubules; wings in most insects.

Hippos: huge barrel-bodied semi-aquatic artiodactyls with eyes, ears and nostrils on top of the head, webbed toes, a near-hairless skin secreting a red sunscreen fluid, enlarged tusk-like canines and incisors, and a three-chambered non-ruminating stomach.

Predatory or blood-feeding annelids with a fixed 34-segment body, an anterior and a large posterior sucker, no chaetae, a reduced coelom filled with tissue, a clitellum, and (in many) anticoagulant saliva.

Chimaeras ('ratfish'): the upper jaw fused to the braincase (holostyly), tooth plates instead of teeth, a single gill opening under a fleshy operculum, naked skin, a venomous dorsal spine, and a frontal clasper in males.
Fungi together with nucleariid amoebae and the rozellids/Microsporidia; ancestrally filose amoebae with flattened cristae; the fungal chitin wall arises within this clade.

Sea cucumbers: elongated along the oral-aboral axis, lying on one side; the skeleton reduced to microscopic ossicles in a leathery body wall; a ring of feeding tentacles (modified tube feet); respiratory trees; defensive evisceration.

Animals plus choanoflagellates, filastereans and ichthyosporeans; ancestrally a cell with a single flagellum encircled by a collar of microvilli, and a genetic tool-kit for cell adhesion and signalling later expanded in animals.

Great apes and humans: large bodies and brains, no tail, broad flat faces, prolonged childhood and lifespan, complex problem-solving and tool use, and a shoulder/torso built for both climbing and (in some) suspensory or upright postures.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: The human branch after the split from Pan: habitual upright bipedal walking (a forward foramen magnum, S-curved spine, bowl-shaped pelvis, arched non-grasping foot, valgus knee), small canines, and later a greatly enlarged brain, language and cumulative culture.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: African great apes and humans: gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans; shared cranial and dental features and knuckle-walking ancestry (retained by gorillas and chimps), from which the human bipedal lineage diverged.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Chimpanzees and bonobos together with humans and their extinct bipedal relatives (australopiths, Homo); the branch on which habitual terrestrial bipedalism, reduced canines and, later, large brains evolved.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Apes: no external tail, a broad flat chest with the shoulder blades on the back, very mobile shoulder and wrist joints (from an ancestry of arm-hanging), a shortened lumbar spine, an appendix, larger brains, and Y-5 molar cusp patterns.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Medusozoans usually with a colonial polyp stage and small medusae budded from the body wall (not by strobilation); the medusa has a true velum; gonads are epidermal; includes Hydra, siphonophores and fire corals.

Gibbons ('lesser apes'): small, slender, monogamous apes that brachiate beneath branches with extremely long arms and hook grips at high speed, sing loud territorial duets, and have 44 chromosomes (unusually variable across genera).
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Quillworts (Isoetes): a squat corm-like stem bearing a rosette of grass-like quill leaves, each with a sporangium sunk in its swollen base; heterosporous; CAM photosynthesis in aquatic species; the last survivors of the giant lycopod (Lepidodendron) lineage.
Free-living bacterivorous biflagellates with a ventral feeding groove; retain the most gene-rich, bacteria-like mitochondrial genomes known in eukaryotes.

Rabbits, hares and pikas: a second small peg-like pair of upper incisors directly behind the first, a herbivorous hindgut-fermenting diet with re-ingestion of soft faeces (caecotrophy), a fenestrated (lattice-like) skull, and side-to-side chewing.

The lamiid (euasterid I) clade: mints, nightshades (tomato, potato), coffee and gentians, borages, olives; usually opposite leaves, corollas that fuse late, and often a two-carpel ovary and specialised alkaloids.
A large placental clade of Laurasian origin - insectivores (shrews, moles), bats, carnivores, pangolins and hoofed mammals (including whales); united chiefly by molecular data.

Strepsirrhines that reached Madagascar and radiated there in isolation: a tooth-comb, a grooming claw, scent-marking, often female social dominance, and body forms from mouse-sized to (extinct) gorilla-sized.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Reptiles with overlapping horny scales shed in patches or whole, a transverse cloacal slit, paired hemipenes in males (or none), and (in squamates) determinate skull kinesis; tuatara plus lizards and snakes.

All cellular life descended from LUCA: a double-stranded DNA genome transcribed to RNA and translated by ribosomes; a nearly universal genetic code; ATP as energy currency; phospholipid-bilayer membranes.

Monocots (Liliales and lily-like relatives) with showy flowers in threes, often six tepals and six stamens, a superior ovary, bulbs or corms, and typically nectar- and pollen-rewarding insect pollination.

Living amphibians (Lissamphibia): a moist, permeable, glandular skin used in gas exchange, pedicellate bicuspid teeth, a papilla amphibiorum in the ear, green rods in the retina, and (usually) an aquatic larva that metamorphoses.
Spiralians characterised by a ciliated tentacular feeding crown (lophophore) in some groups and/or a trochophore larva; molluscs, annelids, brachiopods, bryozoans, nemerteans.

Slow-climbing nocturnal strepsirrhines of Africa and Asia: a very slow deliberate hand-over-hand gait (lorises) or leaping (galagos), a powerful grasp with a reduced index finger, a tooth-comb, and a retia mirabilia in the limbs that resists fatigue.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Homosporous clubmosses (Lycopodium and relatives): trailing or erect stems clothed in small microphylls, upright spore cones, a long-lived underground gametophyte fed by fungi, and spores once sold as flash powder.

The oldest living vascular-plant lineage - clubmosses, spikemosses, quillworts: small single-veined leaves (microphylls), sporangia borne singly on the upper leaf surface (often in cones), and roots that branch by equal forking; Carboniferous tree forms built the coal swamps.

Core angiosperms that are neither monocots nor eudicots: mostly aromatic woody plants (magnolias, laurels, nutmeg, black pepper, avocado) with flower parts in threes, pollen with a single aperture, and often beetle pollination.
The malvid (eurosid II) clade: mallows and cotton, mustards and capers, citrus, myrtles and eucalypts, sumac and cashew; many produce glucosinolate or terpene chemical defences.

Amniotes with hair, mammary glands nursing the young with milk, three middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) and a single lower-jaw bone (dentary), heterodont teeth replaced once, a muscular diaphragm, and endothermy.
Arthropods bearing a pair of mandibles for biting/chewing, one or two pairs of maxillae, antennae on the first head segment, and (ancestrally) compound eyes with a crystalline cone.

Eusporangiate marattioid ferns: large tropical plants with massive fleshy fronds, swollen starchy stipule-buttressed bases, sporangia fused into synangia, and a long-lived fleshy gametophyte; relicts of a Carboniferous tree-fern lineage.

Bryophytes that are either flat dorsiventral thalli or leafy shoots with leaves in three ranks (the underside row reduced); oil bodies in the cells; a capsule that splits into four valves; no stomata (thalloid forms have air pores).

Therians that give birth to tiny embryonic young which finish development attached to a teat, usually in a pouch (marsupium); epipubic bones; a choriovitelline (yolk-sac) placenta; a distinctive tooth count and inflected jaw angle.
Cnidarians whose life cycle includes a free medusa budded from the polyp; a velum or velarium aids jet propulsion; linear mitochondrial chromosomes.
The 'core' flowering plants (~99.9% of species) - monocots, eudicots, magnoliids, Chloranthales and Ceratophyllales - diverging from each other in a rapid burst in the Early Cretaceous.

Anaerobic/microaerophilic flagellates that have lost classical mitochondria (reduced to hydrogenosomes or mitosomes); often many flagella and a stiff cytoskeletal axostyle; includes Giardia, Trichomonas and gut parabasalids.

Multicellular heterotrophs that develop from an embryo; cells without walls, joined by cell junctions over a collagen basement membrane; shared adhesion and signalling proteins (cadherins, integrins); ancestrally with nerve and muscle cells.
Unsegmented coelomates with a muscular foot, a dorsal visceral mass covered by a mantle that secretes a calcareous shell, a mantle cavity with gills (ctenidia), and usually a rasping radula.

Flowering plants with a single seed leaf (cotyledon), leaves with parallel veins and sheathing bases, flower parts in threes, pollen with one aperture, scattered vascular bundles with no cambium (so rarely truly woody), and a fibrous root system.

Egg-laying mammals: a single cloacal opening, a leathery-shelled egg, milk oozing from mammary patches (no nipples), a reptile-like shoulder girdle, electroreceptive bills/snouts, and venom spurs in males (functional in the platypus).

Fast-growing moulds with wide, largely septum-free (coenocytic) hyphae: sexual reproduction by a thick-walled zygospore where two hyphae fuse, and asexual spores made in a stalked sac (sporangium); bread mould Rhizopus; some form plant root symbioses.

Weasels, otters, badgers, raccoons, skunks and the red panda: mostly small, short-legged, elongated caniforms with well-developed anal scent glands (extreme in skunks), often high metabolic rates and delayed implantation, ranging from hypercarnivores to omnivores and the bamboo-eating red panda.
Terrestrial mandibulates with a head plus a long homonomous trunk of many leg-bearing segments, one pair of antennae, tracheae, malpighian tubules, and Toemoesvary organs for sensing humidity.
Baleen whales: keratin baleen plates hanging from the upper jaw to filter small prey from water, paired blowholes, a symmetrical skull, no teeth as adults, and the largest body sizes of any animal.

Jawless cyclostomes that secrete enormous amounts of defensive slime; a partial cranium but no vertebrae or eyes lens; a single nasohypophyseal duct opening to the pharynx; knotting behaviour; burrowing scavengers.
Microscopic endoparasites of fish and annelids; the animal is reduced to spores of a few cells bearing coiled polar filaments; among the smallest animal genomes; no gut, nerves or body axis.

The only living cephalopods that keep a large external coiled shell divided into gas-filled buoyancy chambers linked by a siphuncle; up to ~90 small suckerless tentacles; pinhole eyes with no lens; a leathery hood; slow-growing and long-lived - 'living fossils'.

Unsegmented round worms with a tough collagen cuticle moulted four times, only longitudinal body-wall muscle (so they thrash sinusoidally), a fluid-filled pseudocoel at high pressure, and eutely (fixed cell number).
~95% of living bird species; a near-instantaneous radiation across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, so there is no single skeletal synapomorphy for the whole clade.

Neognathous ('new') palate: a mobile, kinetic palate with a reduced vomer, reduced or absent basipterygoid processes and a flexible pterygoid-palatine joint, allowing cranial kinesis of the upper bill.
Molecular clade uniting Bikonta/Diaphoretickes with Scotokaryotes; no morphological synapomorphy.
Bilaterians with dedicated excretory organs (protonephridia or metanephridia) and, ancestrally, a through-gut with mouth and anus and a coelom; splits into protostomes and deuterostomes.
Opisthokonta plus Breviatea and Apusomonadida; ancestrally biflagellate gliding cells; molecularly defined.
Colonial anthozoans whose polyps always have exactly eight pinnate (feathered) tentacles and eight mesenteries; an internal skeleton of separate calcite sclerites; soft corals, sea fans and sea pens.

Eight-armed coleoids - octopuses and the vampire squid - with the shell lost or vestigial, suckers usually without stalks, the most elaborate brains and camera eyes of any invertebrate, skin chromatophores for instant camouflage, and (in octopuses) a benthic, den-dwelling life.

Toothed whales, dolphins and porpoises: a single blowhole, an asymmetrical skull, homodont conical teeth (or few), and biosonar produced by nasal air sacs and focused through a fatty forehead 'melon'.
Tunicates plus vertebrates; an expanded forebrain region with paired sensory placodes (olfactory and otic), migratory neural-crest-like cells, and a muscular pumping heart.

Whisk ferns (Psilotum) and adder's-tongue ferns (Ophioglossum): Psilotum has no true roots or leaves and dichotomously forking green stems with three-lobed synangia; Ophioglossum bears a single fertile spike and holds the record for chromosome number.
Brittle stars: a sharply set-off central disc and long, snake-like jointed arms moved by 'vertebral' ossicles; tube feet without suckers, used for feeding not walking; the arms writhe for locomotion.

Cells that ancestrally swim with a single posterior flagellum and have flattened mitochondrial cristae; animals + fungi + their protist relatives; a fused multifunctional CAD gene is a molecular signature.

The largest plant family (Orchidaceae): bilaterally symmetric flowers with a landing-pad lip (labellum), stamens and style fused into a column, pollen in sticky masses (pollinia), dust-like seeds with no endosperm needing fungal partners to germinate, and CAM or epiphytic habits in many.
A semi-aquatic monotreme with a soft electroreceptive duck-like bill, dense waterproof fur, webbed forefeet, a beaver-like tail, no teeth as an adult (horny pads), and a venomous ankle spur in males.
Molecular clade joining the jakobids to all 'higher' eukaryotes (Neokaryotes); no unique morphological synapomorphy.
The basidiomycete clade uniting the smut fungi (Ustilaginomycotina) with the mushroom-forming fungi (Agaricomycotina); a molecular grouping within Basidiomycota.

Bony fishes (and their tetrapod descendants): an ossified endoskeleton, dermal bones roofing the skull and forming jaw margins, lungs or a swim bladder from the gut, and (ancestrally) enamel-covered ganoid scales.
Palaeognathous ('ancient') palate: a rigid, robust bony palate with a large vomer bracing the pterygoid-palatine complex and prominent basipterygoid processes.

Pan paniscus: the southern species of Pan, restricted to forests south of the Congo River; more gracile, female-centred and egalitarian, using frequent socio-sexual contact to defuse tension, with little lethal aggression.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Pan troglodytes: the more widespread, northern species of Pan, living in male-bonded communities with lethal territorial aggression, extensive tool kits (termite-fishing, nut-cracking), cooperative hunting of monkeys, and regional behavioural 'cultures'.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: The clade of crustaceans plus hexapods (insects); shared neural and eye developmental characters and a nauplius-type larva ancestrally.

Cryptomonads and their close relatives (kathablepharids, Palpitomonas); cryptomonads keep a nucleomorph (a relict red-algal nucleus) in the plastid, plus ejectisomes and a periplast of surface plates.

The genus Pan - chimpanzees and bonobos: knuckle-walking African apes with fission-fusion societies, tool use, hunting and food sharing, a swollen sexual skin in females, and ~98.8% genome identity with humans.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Placozoans, cnidarians and bilaterians; possess ParaHox genes and an expanded Hox / NK homeobox tool-kit used to pattern the body axis.

Anisodactyl feet (three toes forward, one strong back toe) with an incumbent hallux and a tendon-locking perching mechanism; aegithognathous palate; a derived deep-plantar tendon arrangement; small body; altricial nestlings; distinctive coiled sperm.

'Shape-shifting' amoeboflagellates that switch between crawling amoeba and swimming flagellate forms; discoid mitochondrial cristae; eruptive lobose pseudopods; includes the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria.

Odd-toed ungulates: body weight borne on the central (third) toe, a hindgut fermentation system in an enlarged caecum and colon, relatively simple stomach, and continuously growing (hypsodont) cheek teeth in grazers.

Jawless cyclostomes with a toothed sucker-disc mouth and piston-like tongue used to rasp flesh or attach; seven pairs of gill pouches; a well-developed eye and pineal eye; a larval (ammocoete) filter-feeding stage.

Pangolins: toothless insectivores covered in large overlapping scales of agglutinated hair, a long sticky tongue rooted near the pelvis, powerful digging foreclaws, no teeth (food ground in a keratinous 'gizzard' stomach), and the ability to roll into a ball.

Zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two back); strong chisel- or shovel-shaped bill; obligate cavity nesters laying white eggs; blind naked chicks with prominent heel pads. Woodpeckers add a reinforced skull, stiff prop tail and a very long wrap-around hyoid.
Tiny (<3 um) marine heterotrophic flagellates whose cell is split by a groove into two compartments; feed on colloidal organic matter; have secondarily lost any plastid.
The 'hairy' xenarthrans: anteaters and sloths; no armour, reduced or absent dentition, powerful curved claws requiring a knuckle- or edge-walking gait, and a very low metabolic rate.

Marine caniform carnivorans - seals, sea lions, walrus - with all four limbs modified into flippers, a streamlined blubber-insulated body, reduced external ears or none, and the ability to nurse and haul out on land or ice.

Cone-bearing gymnosperms: mostly evergreen trees with needle or scale leaves, resin canals, wood of tracheids with bordered pits, seeds on woody cone scales (or in a fleshy aril), and dominance of cold and dry forests.

Titis, sakis and uakaris: seed-predator ('sclerocarnivore') New World monkeys with splayed, procumbent lower canines and robust premolars for cracking hard unripe fruit and seeds; a non-prehensile, often bushy tail.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Sakis, bearded sakis and uakaris: seed-predator New World monkeys with splayed, forward-tilted lower canines and thick enamel for prying open and cracking hard unripe fruit and seeds; a non-prehensile, often bushy tail; agile trunk-to-trunk leaping.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Land plants (embryophytes): a multicellular diploid embryo retained and nourished on the parent (hence 'embryophyte'), alternation of generations with a sporophyte, a waxy cuticle with stomata, sporopollenin-walled spores, and sex organs (archegonia and antheridia) with a protective jacket of cells.

Flatworms: dorsoventrally flattened, unsegmented, with no coelom, no anus (a branched blind gut or none), gas exchange across the skin, protonephridia with flame cells, and strong powers of regeneration.

New World monkeys: side-facing nostrils set wide apart, three premolars per quadrant, an ear region without a bony tube, exclusively arboreal, many with a prehensile tail; the only anthropoids that colonised the Americas.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Side-necked turtles: the neck folds horizontally to tuck the head sideways under the shell rim; the pelvis is fused to both carapace and plastron; freshwater, Southern Hemisphere (South America, Africa, Australia).

Grasses (Poaceae): hollow jointed stems (culms), two-ranked leaves with a split sheath and a small ligule, wind-pollinated flowers reduced to florets in spikelets, a single-seeded grain (caryopsis), silica bodies, and growth from the leaf base so they regrow after grazing or fire.
Molecular clade (Amoebozoa + Obazoa + CRuMs) whose members ancestrally make pseudopodia ('feet') from a single anterior region; no strict morphological synapomorphy.

Leptosporangiate ferns - ~90% of living fern species: each sporangium develops from a single cell and has a spring-loaded annulus that catapults the spores; many diversified in the shade of angiosperm forests in the Cretaceous.

Monilophytes: vascular spore plants with megaphylls that unroll from a coiled fiddlehead (circinate vernation), sporangia usually grouped in sori on the leaf underside, a free-living heart-shaped gametophyte, and swimming sperm.
A single species that parasitises the eggs of sturgeon and paddlefish; its free-living stage is an inside-out, tentacled 'stolon' that walks on its tentacles; retains true nematocysts.

Orangutans: the only exclusively Asian great apes and the most arboreal, moving by cautious four-handed climbing; pronounced sexual dimorphism with flanged adult males; very long inter-birth intervals; largely solitary; a fruit-tracking mental map of the forest.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Sessile filter-feeders with no true tissues, nerves or muscles; water is pumped by flagellated choanocyte chambers from surface pores to an osculum; a skeleton of mineral spicules and/or spongin; totipotent archaeocytes.

Mammals with grasping hands and feet bearing flat nails and an opposable thumb/big toe, sensitive friction-ridged pads, forward-facing eyes in bony orbits giving stereoscopic vision, a reduced sense of smell, a large brain, and few, slow-developing offspring.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Bilaterians in which (ancestrally) the blastopore becomes the mouth, cleavage is spiral, the mesoderm forms by schizocoely, and the main nerve cords run ventrally with a circumoesophageal ring.

Strongly down-curved hooked bill with a mobile craniofacial hinge (prokinesis) and a broad fleshy cere; thick prehensile tongue; zygodactyl feet used like hands to manipulate food; large head and brain; powder down.
Parrots + passerines: greatly enlarged forebrain, high cognition and (convergently, in true parrots and oscines) learned vocalisation controlled by dedicated forebrain song nuclei.

Mostly the rust fungi: obligate biotrophic plant parasites with the most complex life cycles known in fungi - up to five spore types and, in many, an obligatory alternation between two unrelated host plants; simple septal pores, no clamp connections.

Sauropsid amniotes with scaly skin of beta-keratin, uricotelic excretion, a largely three-chambered heart (four-chambered in archosaurs), and eggs with little yolk-free albumen; ancestrally ectothermic.

Rhinoceroses: massive herbivores with one or two keratin horns (no bony core) on the midline of the snout, thick protective skin, three toes per foot, columnar legs, and poor eyesight offset by acute hearing and smell.
Lungfishes plus tetrapods; functional lungs used for air-breathing, internal nostrils (choanae) in the tetrapod line, and a two-part fin/limb skeleton beyond the first bone.
The red-algal lineage together with Picozoa and the predatory rhodelphids; ancestrally with phycobilisome light-harvesting antennae.

Red algae: light-harvesting phycobiliproteins on phycobilisomes, floridean starch stored in the cytoplasm, unstacked thylakoids, pit connections between cells, and no flagella or centrioles at any life stage.

Represented today only by the tuatara (Sphenodon) of New Zealand: a lizard-like reptile keeping a complete lower temporal bar, a beak-like premaxilla, teeth fused to the jaw edge in a single wedge row (acrodont), a well-developed parietal 'third eye', very slow growth, and no copulatory organ.

The most species-rich mammal order: one pair of continuously growing incisors per jaw backed by hard enamel only on the front, powerful specialised jaw muscles (masseter) threaded through the skull, a diastema, and generally small size and high fecundity.

One of the two big eudicot clades (~25% of angiosperms): often woody, with flowers whose petals are separate, many stamens, and a tendency to nitrogen-fixing root symbioses; includes legumes, roses, oaks, mustards, mallows, eucalypts.

The earliest-branching fungi - rozellids (Cryptomycota) and Microsporidia: extreme intracellular parasites, mostly without a chitin wall in the feeding stage; Microsporidia have among the smallest eukaryotic genomes, mitosomes instead of mitochondria, and infect hosts by firing a coiled polar tube.

Cud-chewing artiodactyls with a four-chambered stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) and foregut microbial fermentation, no upper incisors (a horny dental pad instead), and usually bony horns or antlers; deer, cattle, antelope, giraffes.

A major molecular clade - Stramenopiles (diatoms, brown algae, oomycetes), Alveolates (dinoflagellates, ciliates, apicomplexan parasites) and Rhizaria (foraminifera, radiolarians); no morphological synapomorphy, though many share plastids of red-algal secondary origin and tubular mitochondrial cristae.

The great majority of Ascomycota: the budding yeasts (Saccharomyces - baking, brewing, biology) plus the Pezizomycotina, filamentous ascomycetes that build true fruiting bodies and include most lichen fungi, many plant pathogens, and the penicillin and cephalosporin producers.

Small slender cebids with a long non-prehensile tail used for balance, a short close 'gothic arch' of white facial fur around dark muzzle and eyes, very large brain relative to body, and large mixed-sex troops.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Lobe-finned fishes and tetrapods: paired fins/limbs with a single proximal bone articulating with the girdle and muscular, bony fin lobes; cosmoid scales ancestrally; enamel on the teeth.

Treeshrews: small squirrel-like Southeast Asian mammals with a long snout, sharp insectivore teeth, claws (not nails), a large brain-to-body ratio, and the highest metabolic rate relative to size of any mammal; 'absentee' parental care.

Arachnids with large grasping pedipalp pincers, a segmented tail (metasoma) ending in a venomous sting, comb-like pectines under the body, and fluorescence under UV light; ancient, little changed since the Silurian.
Molecular clade uniting Amorphea with Metamonada and CRuMs (broadly, the non-photosynthetic 'opisthokont side' of eukaryotes); no morphological synapomorphy.
The laurasiatheres outside Eulipotyphla (bats, carnivores, pangolins, ungulates); named for the ancestral presence of a post-penile scrotum; a molecular clade.
'True jellyfish': a large dominant medusa and a reduced polyp (scyphistoma) that releases young medusae by transverse strobilation; gastric filaments; four-part symmetry; rhopalia as sense organs.
Modern sharks: a fusiform body, pectoral fins not fused to the head, gill slits on the sides, a heterocercal tail, and highly protrusible jaws in most.

Spikemosses (Selaginella): creeping stems with four ranks of microphylls each bearing a tiny flap (ligule), heterospory (two spore sizes), roots on leafless branchlets (rhizophores), and desiccation tolerance in the 'resurrection plants'.

Monkeys and apes (anthropoids): a fused frontal bone and lower-jaw symphysis, a bony back wall to the eye socket, dry nose, forward fovea and full colour vision in many, larger brains, and generally diurnal, social life.
Tags: animals chordates eukaryotes mammals primates vertebrates

Traits: Seed plants: reproduction by seeds (a dormant embryo packaged with food and a protective coat), pollen carrying the male gametes so no water is needed for fertilisation, a much-reduced gametophyte kept inside the parent, ovules, and wood from a bifacial cambium in most.
Protostomes ancestrally with spiral cleavage and, in many, a trochophore larva; body surface ciliated; includes molluscs, annelids, flatworms, brachiopods and rotifers.

Lizards, snakes and amphisbaenians: a highly kinetic skull that has lost the lower temporal bar, paired eversible hemipenes, a forked or notched tongue serving a Jacobson's (vomeronasal) organ, skin shed periodically, and (ancestrally) the ability to shed the tail to escape.
'Stalked jellyfish' with no free-swimming medusa: a funnel-shaped body attached by an adhesive basal disc, combining polyp and medusa features, with eight clusters of knobbed tentacles.

'Wet-nosed' primates - lemurs, lorises, galagos: a moist rhinarium and split upper lip tethered to the gum, a reflective tapetum lucidum for night vision, a tooth-comb of procumbent lower front teeth for grooming, and a grooming claw on the second toe.

Traits: Charophyte green algae plus land plants; a broadened, asymmetrical flagellar root with a multilayered structure, and biochemical traits (class-I aldolase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, glycolate oxidase) shared with land plants.

Huge forward-facing eyes locked in sclerotic tubes; a facial disc of stiff feathers funnelling sound to often asymmetrical ear openings; silent flight from comb-fringed, velvety flight feathers; reversible outer toe; nocturnal.
Aerial insectivores and nectarivores with a tiny bill but very wide gape; small weak feet and short legs; ancestrally nocturnal/crepuscular; many use torpor; long pointed wings.

Pigs and peccaries: non-ruminant omnivores with a simple stomach, a mobile cartilage-reinforced snout disc for rooting, bunodont (low, rounded-cusped) molars, continuously growing canine tusks, and four toes with the outer two not reaching the ground.
The fungi defined by ancient plant symbiosis: the arbuscular mycorrhizal Glomeromycota plus the Dikarya; ancestrally associated with land plants.

Terrestrial monotremes ('spiny anteaters') covered in protective spines, with a tubular toothless snout, a long sticky tongue for ants and termites, powerful digging claws, and a temporary pouch that holds the egg.

An early-diverging, mostly simple ascomycete grade: no fruiting body; includes the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces (a model organism), the plant pathogen Taphrina (peach leaf curl), and Pneumocystis, a cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised people.

Tapirs: pig-like browsers with a short prehensile proboscis formed from the nose and upper lip, four toes in front and three behind, a stocky body for pushing through forest, and striped-and-spotted young.

Tiny nocturnal Southeast Asian haplorhines: enormous immobile eyes (each about as large as the brain) in a neck that rotates ~180 deg, elongated tarsal (ankle) bones for prodigious leaping, entirely carnivorous diet, and long grasping fingers with rounded pads.

Traits: 'Core landbirds'; ancestrally arboreal with a raptorial common ancestor hypothesised (strong grasping feet, hooked bill); altricial, nest-bound young.

Turtles: a shell of fused ribs and vertebrae (carapace) plus a plastron, with the limb girdles uniquely inside the ribcage; no teeth (a horny beak); the neck retracted sideways (pleurodires) or vertically (cryptodires).

Four-limbed vertebrates with digits, a neck separating head from pectoral girdle (shoulder freed from the skull), a sacrum anchoring the pelvis to the spine, distinct wrist/ankle joints, and lungs as the primary adult respiration.

Live-bearing mammals (marsupials + placentals): no shelled egg, nipples for suckling, a mobile scapula with the coracoid reduced to a process, teeth replaced in only one set of positions, and (ancestrally) three-cusped molars of tribosphenic form.
The only palaeognaths that fly: a fully keeled sternum and functional flight muscles retained; compact ground-dwelling body, very short tail, cryptic plumage; males incubate.

Vascular plants: lignified water-conducting xylem (tracheids/vessels) and sugar-conducting phloem, a dominant branched sporophyte with true roots and (usually) leaves, and stomatal control of gas exchange.

Marine filter-feeders (sea squirts, salps) enclosed in a cellulose 'tunic'; a tadpole larva with notochord and nerve cord that is usually resorbed at metamorphosis into a sessile adult with a huge pharyngeal basket.

Bears: the largest land carnivorans, plantigrade with five non-retractile claws, a short tail and long snout; flat crushing molars and reduced carnassials for a mostly omnivorous or herbivorous diet (the polar bear reverted to meat); delayed implantation and winter denning.

Smut fungi: biotrophic parasites mainly of grasses and cereals that replace the host's flowers or grains with sooty masses of thick-walled teliospores; a dimorphic life cycle switching between a harmless yeast and an infectious filament; intracellular but not killing host cells.

Anteaters: a toothless tubular skull, a long protrusible worm-like tongue flicked rapidly and coated in sticky saliva, huge digging foreclaws (walking on the knuckles), a low body temperature, and a keen sense of smell.

Chordates with a bony or cartilaginous vertebral column around the nerve cord, a cranium enclosing a tripartite brain, paired special sense organs, neural crest, ectodermal placodes, and a chambered heart.
The green lineage (green algae + land plants): chlorophyll a and b, plastids with stacked thylakoids and no phycobilisomes, starch stored inside the plastid, and cellulose-rich cell walls.

A single family (Vitaceae) - grapes and Virginia creeper: climbing shrubs with leaf-opposed tendrils, swollen leaf-base nodes, small four/five-parted flowers with a nectar disc, and a berry fruit; sister to the rest of the rosids.

Hippopotamuses plus cetaceans (whales, dolphins): the closest living relatives of whales among land mammals; shared traits include hairlessness, aquatic or semi-aquatic habits, giving birth and suckling in water, and loss of sebaceous (sweat) glands.

Small simple worms with no through-gut (a blind sac or none), no discrete excretory organs, a basiepidermal nerve net or paired cords, and a distinctive ciliary rootlet; includes acoels and Xenoturbella.

South American placentals with extra ('xenarthrous') articulations between the lumbar vertebrae, a low metabolic rate and low body temperature, simplified peg-like teeth without enamel (or none), and often bony dermal armour.
Marine chelicerates with a large horseshoe-shaped carapace, a hinged opisthosoma, book gills, a long spike-like telson, and blue copper-based haemolymph; 'living fossils'.
The other main bat clade: all laryngeally echolocating, mostly insectivorous families (vesper bats, free-tailed bats, leaf-nosed bats of the New World, true vampire bats).
One of the two main bat clades: the large non-echolocating Old World fruit bats plus several echolocating families (horseshoe bats, false vampires); some fruit bats use tongue-click echolocation.

An early non-flagellated fungal clade of parasites and predators of small animals, amoebae and other fungi - e.g. Entomophthora, which manipulates and kills flies, and trap-forming predators of nematodes; often forcibly discharged spores.
